y-m-10-01.title: Which village has more people?
y-m-10-01.topic: Comparing large numbers (number of digits, then comparing from the highest place)
y-m-10-01.goal: Explain how the size is decided when the numbers have different numbers of digits, and which place's digit decides the result when they have the same number of digits. Decide what you need to know in order to compare when a digit is hidden.
y-m-10-01.material: You want to compare the number of people living in Garam Village (가람마을) and Narae Village (나래마을). The numbers on the sign are all natural numbers, they are written with a comma (,) after every three digits, and the first digit is not 0. The unit is '명' (people).
y-m-10-01.thinking.0: Decide whether there is enough information to compare
y-m-10-01.thinking.1: Explain, using an if-then sentence, why we compare from the highest place
y-m-10-01.thinking.2: Tell apart 'the exact value' and 'enough information to compare'
y-m-10-01.prereq.0: Place values and reading of large numbers up to the millions (4th-grade level)
y-m-10-01.prereq.1: Reading numbers written with commas after every three digits
y-m-10-01.s.s1.prompt: First, a case where all the digits can be seen. Garam Village has 987,654 people (nine hundred eighty-seven thousand six hundred fifty-four) and Narae Village has 1,000,000 people (one million). Which village has more people?
y-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.0: Count the digits to see how many digits each number has.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how much you must add to 987,654 to get 1,000,000, and look at the difference between the two numbers.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.a: Garam Village. Big digits like 9, 8, 7 come first, so it is bigger
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.a: You looked at how big the first digits are. Check whether the same method works both when the two numbers have the same number of digits and when they have different numbers of digits.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.b: Narae Village. Garam Village has a six-digit number and Narae Village has a seven-digit number
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of counting the number of digits first, rather than looking at each digit.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.o.c: Cannot decide. The groups separated by commas are different in number, so they cannot be compared
y-m-10-01.s.s1.r.c: You thought the numbers cannot be compared if the comma groups differ. Commas are only marks that make numbers easier to read. Think about what decides the size of a number.
y-m-10-01.s.s1.explain: For natural numbers whose first digit is not 0, the one with more digits is bigger. 987,654 is a six-digit number and 1,000,000 is a seven-digit number. Even if the front digits 9, 8, 7 look big, it does not help. You can also check this because adding 12,346 to 987,654 gives 1,000,000.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.prompt: This time the sign got a smudge. Garam Village has 3,□45,678 people (□ is one hidden digit in the hundred-thousands place), and Narae Village has 3,500,000 people (three million five hundred thousand). What do you need to know to decide which village has more?
y-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the two numbers side by side, one place at a time from the highest place, and find the first place where the digits differ.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try putting 0 and 9 in □ and check whether which village has more changes.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.a: Garam Village's number has 45,678 in the back part and Narae Village's back part is 00,000, so Garam Village has more even without knowing □
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.a: You compared the numbers by their back parts. If the front digits differ in the same place, the back parts do not affect the result. Put 0 in □ and compare directly.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.b: You can decide only if you know exactly what □ is
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.b: You thought you must know the exact value of □. Try putting in a few digits for □ to test whether knowing only a range is enough to compare.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.c: Knowing only whether □ is 4 or less, or 5 or more, is enough to decide
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.c: You found the boundary where the comparison result changes, and described the needed information as a 'range', not a 'value'.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.o.d: Even without knowing □, compare the ones place: Garam Village's 8 is greater than Narae Village's 0, so Garam Village has more
y-m-10-01.s.s2.r.d: You compared starting from the lowest place. Think about which place you should look at first when comparing large numbers.
y-m-10-01.s.s2.explain: The millions place of both numbers is 3, so compare the next place, the hundred-thousands place. Narae Village has 5. If □ is 6~9, Garam Village has more, and if □ is 0~4, Narae Village has more. If □ is 5, the hundred-thousands places are equal, so look at the next place. The ten-thousands place is 4 for Garam Village and 0 for Narae Village, so Garam Village has more (3,545,678 > 3,500,000). So even without knowing exactly what □ is, knowing just 'is it 4 or less, or 5 or more?' is enough to decide.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.prompt: The result changes depending on the digit in □. Using conditions like 'if □ is ...', write in which cases Garam Village has more and in which cases Narae Village has more. Also write which place you compared to decide that.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number with 5 in □ and Narae Village's number side by side, starting from the highest place.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write which village has more when □ is 4 and when □ is 6.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you look separately at what happens when □ is 5?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your answer show the order: the millions place is equal, so the next place was compared?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check your cases by putting real digits (for example, 2 and 7) into □?
y-m-10-01.s.s3.model.0: If □ is 5 or a greater number, Garam Village has more, and if □ is 4 or a smaller number, Narae Village has more. The millions place is 3 in both, so I compared □ in the hundred-thousands place with 5.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.model.1: When □ is 4 or less, Narae Village has more, and when □ is from 5 to 9, Garam Village has more. The highest place, the millions place, is the same, so I looked at the next place.
y-m-10-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It does not give the reason for including the case □=5 in 5 to 9, but it splits the boundary correctly.

y-m-10-02.title: Seoa's answer: can we trust it?
y-m-10-02.topic: Checking the result of (three-digit number)×(two-digit number) (estimation, ones digit, place alignment)
y-m-10-02.goal: Without redoing the calculation, use estimation and the ones digit to find that the answer is wrong, find the wrong line in the solution and explain why, and make your own multiplication that passes both quick checks.
y-m-10-02.material: One notebook costs 347원. To find the price of 23 notebooks, Seoa did a vertical multiplication and wrote the answer 1,735원. You can see Seoa's calculation in the second step. First, without redoing the calculation, think about whether this answer can be trusted.
y-m-10-02.thinking.0: Judging with reasons whether a result makes sense
y-m-10-02.thinking.2: Finding the first line where the error happens
y-m-10-02.thinking.3: Making your own example that meets the conditions
y-m-10-02.prereq.0: Experience calculating (three-digit number)×(one-digit number) and (two-digit number)×(two-digit number)
y-m-10-02.prereq.1: Experience estimating with nearby numbers in hundreds and tens
y-m-10-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you can use as evidence that Seoa's answer 1,735원 is wrong. (Things you can tell without redoing the calculation from the start)
y-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether you can easily estimate a value close in size to Seoa's answer.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.hint.1: Try changing 347 and 23 to nearby numbers in hundreds and tens, or look at which digits' product decides the ones digit of the product.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.a: 1,735 is a four-digit number and 347×23 also seems to be a four-digit number, so it seems right
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.a: You only looked at the fact that the number of digits is the same. Four-digit numbers range very widely from 1,000 to 9,999, so this is not enough to judge the size.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.b: If you treat 347 as about 300 and 23 as about 20, the answer should be around 300×20=6,000, so 1,735 is too small
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.b: You first estimated the rough size by changing the two numbers being multiplied to nearby numbers in hundreds and tens.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.c: If you calculate once more the same way and get the same value, it is correct
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.c: If you repeat the same method, the same mistake can be repeated. Think about checking with a different method.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.o.d: Since 7×3=21, the ones digit of the product should be 1, but 1,735 ends in 5
y-m-10-02.s.s1.r.d: You used the property that the ones digit of a product is decided by the product of the ones digits.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.explain: b and d reach the same conclusion (it is not 1,735) by different methods. b checks the size and d checks the ones digit. a only says the number of digits is the same, so its evidence is weak, and c can repeat the same mistake. With estimation or the ones-digit check you can be sure it is 'wrong', but even if it passes both, you cannot conclude it is 'right'.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.acc.0: Estimation alone shows that 1,735 is too small. The ones-digit check (d) is also independent evidence.
y-m-10-02.s.s1.acc.1: The ones digit alone shows it is wrong. The estimation that looks at size (b) is another piece of evidence.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.prompt: Read Seoa's solution line by line. Which line is the first wrong one?
y-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether the multiplication and addition on each line are correct.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check which place the 2 in 23 is in, and look at whether the 694 on the second line is placed to match that place.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.line.0: Multiply by the ones digit 3 first. 347 × 3 = 1041, so write 1041 on the first line.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.line.1: Multiply by the tens digit 2. 347 × 2 = 694, so write 694 on the second line, aligned with the right end of the first line.
y-m-10-02.s.s2.explain: The first mistake is on line 2. The 2 in 23 is a tens digit, so it means 20, and you must add 347×20=6940. If you write 694 aligned at the right end, you add 694, not 6940. The addition on line 3 is correct by itself, but the two numbers being added are wrong, and as a result the conclusion on line 4 is also wrong. The correct answer is 1041 + 6940 = 7981.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.prompt: Make two multiplications with different products that pass both the estimation (the product is 6,000 or more and 8,000 or less) and the ones-digit check (the product ends in 1). The multiplicand a is a three-digit number and the multiplier b is a two-digit number. 347×23 has already been used, so do not use it.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.0: The ones digit of a product is the same as the ones digit of the product of the two numbers' ones digits. Find the pairs of digits for which this value is 1.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.hint.1: After choosing the pair of digits, change the three-digit number and the two-digit number and check by estimation whether the product falls between 6,000 and 8,000.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c1: a is a three-digit natural number.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be a natural number from 100 to 999.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c2: b is a two-digit natural number.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c2: b must be a natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c3: The product is 6,000 or more and 8,000 or less.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c3: The product is not between 6,000 and 8,000. Try estimating.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c4: The ones digit of the product is 1.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c4: The ones digit of the product is not 1. Look at the product of the ones digits.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.ok.c5: It is a number other than 347.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.fail.c5: 347×23 has already been used. Choose a different a.
y-m-10-02.s.s3.explain: For example, 301×21=6321 and 249×29=7221 pass both checks. For the ones digit to be 1, the ones digits of the two numbers must be (1, 1), (3, 7), (7, 3), or (9, 9). However, even an answer in which another place was calculated wrongly can pass the same checks. The checks are useful for catching 'wrong' answers, but they do not guarantee 'right'.

y-m-10-03.title: Boxes for 200 apples
y-m-10-03.topic: Interpreting the quotient and remainder of a division with a remainder to fit the situation
y-m-10-03.goal: Understand that the same quotient and remainder are used as different answers when the question changes, and, by making possible numbers for a division with a given quotient and remainder, check the condition 'the remainder is smaller than the divisor'.
y-m-10-03.material: A fruit shop has 200 apples. One box can hold up to 12 apples. 200 divided by 12 gives a quotient of 16 and a remainder of 8 (12×16=192 and 200-192=8).
y-m-10-03.thinking.0: Changing or keeping your judgment according to a new condition
y-m-10-03.thinking.1: Interpreting the same calculation result to fit the situation
y-m-10-03.thinking.2: Making several solutions that meet the conditions
y-m-10-03.thinking.3: Explaining the condition on the size of the remainder
y-m-10-03.prereq.0: The meaning of quotient and remainder in (three-digit number)÷(two-digit number)
y-m-10-03.prereq.1: Experience checking a division with multiplication and addition
y-m-10-03.s.s1.prompt: Follow along, getting one piece of information at a time, to see how the same calculation result (quotient 16, remainder 8) is used depending on the question.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.0: Each time a piece of information is given, explain in words where the 8 apples are.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.hint.1: If each answer is right, check how many apples there are in all by multiplying by 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.info: The owner said, “I want to put the apples in boxes and keep them.” There is nothing else said yet.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many boxes are needed? Choose your thought for now.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If you read “put them in boxes and keep them” to mean putting all of them in, it is 17 boxes, and the thought of first checking what to do with the 8 apples is also reasonable. 16 boxes is an answer that puts the 8 apples nowhere.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You wrote only the quotient as the answer and did not think about what happens to the remaining 8 apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 17 boxes. The remaining 8 apples must be put in too, so one more box is needed
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read it as putting the remaining 8 apples in a box too.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Cannot decide. We need to know what to do with the remaining 8 apples
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You found what information is missing from the question.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.info: The owner added, “I can only sell customers boxes that are full with 12 apples.”
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then how many boxes can be sold to customers?
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.after: There are 16 full boxes, and the 8 apples are left over because they cannot fill a box. In this question, the quotient 16 is the answer.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 17 boxes. A box with the leftover apples can also be sold
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You did not use the new condition you just heard, 'only full boxes'.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 16 boxes. Only full boxes are counted, so it equals the quotient
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You reflected the condition that only 'full boxes' are counted.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 8 boxes. You can sell as many as the remainder
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You read the remainder 8 as the number of boxes. The remainder is the number of leftover apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The owner changed their mind. “Let's not throw away the leftover apples; put them all in boxes and keep them in the warehouse. One box can hold up to 12 apples.”
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many boxes will be kept in the warehouse, and how many apples will be in the last box?
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Of the 17 boxes, 16 hold 12 apples each, which is 192, and the last box holds the remaining 8 apples (192+8=200). To fill all 17 boxes completely you would need 12×17=204 apples, so you would be 4 apples short.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 16 boxes, and 12 apples in the last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You did not decide where to put the remaining 8 apples.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 17 boxes, and 12 apples in the last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You counted the number of boxes correctly, but check how many apples there would be if all 17 boxes were filled completely.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 17 boxes, and 8 apples in the last box
y-m-10-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought of putting the remainder in the last box.
y-m-10-03.s.s1.reflect: At first, both b and c were reasonable (because we did not know what to do with the 8 apples). Depending on the new condition, the answer became 16 or 17. Even with the same calculation result, depending on whether the question is about 'only the full ones' or 'all of them', you use the quotient as it is or add 1 to the quotient.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.prompt: This time, let's think backward. A three-digit number a was divided by a two-digit number b, and the quotient was 15 and the remainder was 17 (division: a ÷ b = 15 … 17). Make two pairs of such a and b, with different values of b.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.0: If the quotient is 15 and the remainder is 17, first try b=20 and find what number has b going in 15 times with 17 left over.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.hint.1: Actually divide the a you made by b to check that you get quotient 15 and remainder 17, and compare the remainder with b.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.ok.c1: b is a two-digit natural number.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c1: b must be a natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.ok.c2: a is a three-digit natural number.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c2: a must be a natural number from 100 to 999.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.ok.c3: b goes in 15 times and 17 is left over.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c3: a is not the number you get by adding 17 to b×15. Try building a backward from the quotient and the remainder.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The remainder 17 is smaller than the divisor.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The remainder 17 is greater than or equal to the divisor b. If you actually divide in this equation, the quotient and remainder change.
y-m-10-03.s.s2.explain: a is b×15+17. For example, if b=20 then a=317, and 317÷20 gives quotient 15 and remainder 17. However, the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so b must be greater than 17, and for a to be a three-digit number, b must be 65 or less. So any natural number b from 18 to 65 works.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.prompt: Minho chose b=12 and a=197 and wrote “197 ÷ 12 = 15 … 17”. Write why this equation cannot be a correct division result, and write the actual quotient and remainder when 197 is divided by 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the number left after taking 12 away from 197 fifteen times with 12.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether you can take 12 away one more time from the leftover number, and then write how the quotient and remainder change.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you look at how many more times 12 goes into the remainder 17?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check the actual quotient and remainder with 12×(quotient)+(remainder)=197?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write in your own words why the remainder must be smaller than the divisor?
y-m-10-03.s.s3.model.0: It is because the remainder 17 is bigger than the divisor 12. 12 goes into 17 one more time, so if you actually do 197÷12, the quotient is 16 and the remainder is 5.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.model.1: The number left after dividing by 12 must be smaller than 12, but 17 is left, so you can divide one more time. So 197 = 12×16 + 5.
y-m-10-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It uses 'the leftover number' instead of the word 'remainder', but means the same thing.

y-m-10-04.title: Fractions with denominator 7 whose whole-number part is 2
y-m-10-04.topic: The relationship between improper fractions and mixed numbers with the same denominator (finding improper fractions with the same whole-number part)
y-m-10-04.goal: Find the wrong line in a fraction solution by estimation (comparing sizes), find all numerators that meet the condition, and generalize what pattern there is. Explain why the boundary cases that become whole numbers are excluded from mixed numbers.
y-m-10-04.material: A proper fraction is a fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator, an improper fraction is a fraction whose numerator is equal to or greater than its denominator, and a mixed number is a number with a whole number and a proper fraction together (example: 2 and 3/7). A fraction that comes out exactly to a whole number, like 14/7, is a whole number, not a mixed number. In this activity, the numerator of a fraction is a natural number.
y-m-10-04.thinking.0: Checking a solution by comparing sizes
y-m-10-04.thinking.1: Making several examples that meet the conditions
y-m-10-04.thinking.2: Judging boundary cases by the definition
y-m-10-04.thinking.3: Reasoning about the counting rule when the denominator changes
y-m-10-04.prereq.0: The names and meanings of proper fractions, improper fractions, and mixed numbers (4th-grade level)
y-m-10-04.prereq.1: Experience changing a whole number into a fraction with the same denominator
y-m-10-04.s.s1.prompt: Hangyeol wrote a solution to change '3 and 2/5' into an improper fraction. Which line is the first wrong one?
y-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.0: First think about which is bigger, 3 and 2/5 or 3, and compare it with the final result of the solution.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.hint.1: First check what fraction with denominator 5 the whole number 1 is.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.line.0: Let's write the whole number 3 in 3 and 2/5 as a fraction with denominator 5.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.line.3: So 3 and 2/5 is equal to 5/5, that is, 1.
y-m-10-04.s.s1.explain: The first mistake is on line 2. 1 is 5/5, so 3 is 15/5. 3/5 is less than 1, so it cannot be equal to 3. The result on line 4 is also wrong, because 3 and 2/5 is greater than 3 but it says 1. The correct solution is to add 15/5 and 2/5 to get 17/5.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.prompt: Among the improper fractions with denominator 7, find three fractions whose whole-number part is 2 when written as a mixed number, and enter their numerators. (In □/7, □ is the numerator. Since it is a mixed number, there must be a proper-fraction part.)
y-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.0: When the numerator is 7, 8, 9, …, change □/7 into a mixed number and write in a table how the whole-number part changes.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.hint.1: From the table, pick only the rows where the whole-number part is 2, compare the numerators, and also check whether a proper-fraction part is left.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator is a natural number.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator must be a natural number that is 1 or more.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator, so it is an improper fraction.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c2: If the numerator is less than 7, it is a proper fraction. Make it an improper fraction.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c3: When changed to a mixed number, the whole-number part is 2.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c3: When changed to a mixed number, the whole-number part is not 2. Look at what □/7 equals 2.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.ok.c4: It has a proper-fraction part, so it is a mixed number.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.fail.c4: It is a number that comes out exactly to a whole number. Choose a numerator that leaves a proper-fraction part.
y-m-10-04.s.s2.explain: 14/7 is the whole number 2, and 21/7 is 3. The mixed numbers whose whole-number part is 2 are 2 and 1/7 through 2 and 6/7, and when changed to improper fractions, there are six, with numerators 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.prompt: This time the denominator is 9. When written as mixed numbers, how many improper fractions have a whole-number part of 2?
y-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.0: When the denominator is 9, write all the numbers that can go in □ in the mixed number 2 and □/9.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check what number you get when □ is 0 or 9, and decide whether to include those two cases.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.o.a: 6. The count is the same even if the denominator changes
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.a: You thought the count for denominator 7 stays the same. Check by listing the numerators yourself for denominator 9.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.b: You included the numerator 18. Check whether 18/9 is a whole number or a mixed number.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.c: You included both end numbers. Check what 18/9 and 27/9 each equal.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.r.d: This is the idea of counting without the two ends, which come out exactly to whole numbers.
y-m-10-04.s.s3.explain: The mixed numbers whose whole-number part is 2 are 2 and 1/9 through 2 and 8/9, which is 8. When changed to improper fractions, the numerators are 19 to 26. 18/9 is 2 and 27/9 is 3, so they are not mixed numbers. The count is 6 when the denominator is 7 and 8 when it is 9, so the count equals (denominator - 1). This is because the numerator of the proper-fraction part can be anything from 1 to (denominator - 1).

y-m-10-05.title: Finding decimal pairs that add up to 1
y-m-10-05.topic: The sum of a one-decimal-place number and a two-decimal-place number (sums by place below the decimal point)
y-m-10-05.goal: Decide whether adding a one-decimal-place number and a two-decimal-place number can make 1, make pairs of two-decimal-place numbers whose sum is 1, and describe what pattern there is in the sums of the digits in each place.
y-m-10-05.material: In this activity, a 'one-decimal-place number' is a number with one digit after the decimal point, like 0.4, and a 'two-decimal-place number' is a number whose second digit after the decimal point is not 0, like 0.35. 0.30 is equal to 0.3, so it counts as a one-decimal-place number. All numbers are greater than 0.
y-m-10-05.thinking.0: Decide first whether it is possible or impossible, and find the evidence
y-m-10-05.thinking.1: Telling apart a few tests and an explanation based on place value
y-m-10-05.thinking.2: Finding a pattern from several examples
y-m-10-05.prereq.0: Place values of one-decimal-place and two-decimal-place numbers (4th-grade level)
y-m-10-05.prereq.1: Experience adding decimals by lining up the decimal points
y-m-10-05.s.s1.prompt: If you add one one-decimal-place number and one two-decimal-place number, is there a pair that makes exactly 1?
y-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.0: Check, one pair at a time, whether 0.4+0.6 and 0.55+0.45 are pairs that fit the agreement of this problem.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one one-decimal-place number and one two-decimal-place number, add them, and write down only the second digit after the decimal point in the sum.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.a: Yes. You can find a pair, like adding 0.4 and 0.6 to get 1
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.a: Reread the agreement to see whether 0.6 is a one-decimal-place number or a two-decimal-place number.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.b: Yes. You can find a pair whose sum is 1, like 0.55 and 0.45
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.b: You found a pair whose sum is 1, but check whether both numbers are the same kind.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.c: No. The second decimal digit of the sum is the same as the second digit of the two-decimal-place number, so it cannot be 0
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.c: You tried to explain by looking separately at the digit in each place after the decimal point.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.o.d: If I add many pairs and it never comes out, I can say there is none, but I have not tried every pair, so I am not sure
y-m-10-05.s.s1.r.d: You made a judgment from the results of a few tests, but you also thought about how certain it is.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.explain: A one-decimal-place number has an empty second decimal place (it is 0). So the second decimal digit of the sum is just the second digit of the two-decimal-place number, and by the agreement that digit is not 0. For the sum to be 1 (= 1.00), the second place would have to be 0, so there is no such pair. Testing many pairs is a good start, and explaining with place value covers all cases at once.
y-m-10-05.s.s1.acc.0: You correctly pointed out that tests alone cannot guarantee 'all cases'. If you can explain with place value, you can say it is certain.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.prompt: This time, find pairs of two two-decimal-place numbers that add up to exactly 1. Both numbers must have a second digit after the decimal point that is not 0. Make three different pairs. (A pair with just the order switched is the same pair.)
y-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one number first, and check that the value you get by subtracting it from 1 does not have 0 in its second place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write each pair you made split into the first and second decimal places, and compare what the sum of the digits is in each place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Both numbers must be greater than 0.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c2: Both numbers go as far as the second decimal place.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c2: There are more than two digits after the decimal point (third place or beyond), or the digits do not fit.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.ok.c3: In both numbers, the second decimal digit is not 0.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.fail.c3: There is a number whose second decimal digit is 0 (example: 0.4). 0.4 is a one-decimal-place number.
y-m-10-05.s.s2.explain: There are pairs like 0.35+0.65, 0.12+0.88, and 0.99+0.01. The one-decimal-place numbers 0.4 and 0.6 do not fit this agreement. If one number's second decimal digit is 5, the other number's second digit must also be 5 (5+5=10).
y-m-10-05.s.s3.prompt: In pairs whose sum is 1, what do you get when you add the first-decimal-place digits together and the second-decimal-place digits together? Use one pair you made as an example and write the pattern.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write one pair you made lined up vertically, and add the first-decimal-place digits and the second-decimal-place digits separately.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.hint.1: Test whether other pairs give the same values.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write clearly that the sum of the first places and the sum of the second places are different values?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test whether the pattern works for pairs other than the one you chose?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain what happens in the first place when the sum of the second places is 10?
y-m-10-05.s.s3.model.0: The first-decimal-place digits add up to 9, and the second-decimal-place digits add up to 10. For 0.35 and 0.65, it is also 3+6=9 and 5+5=10.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.model.1: The second places add up to 10, so 1 is carried to the first place, and the first places add up to 9, so receiving 1 makes 10, which carries 1 more to give 1. I checked with 0.12 and 0.88.
y-m-10-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer explains the pattern with carrying.

y-m-10-06.title: Can three months of records tell us next month?
y-m-10-06.topic: Skip counting with large numbers and the limits of predicting by a rule
y-m-10-06.goal: Predict the next number from a record that skip counts by 100,000, but show with a counterexample that a few records cannot make it 'certainly' so, and tell apart a prediction from certainty.
y-m-10-06.material: An amusement park recorded the number of visitors each month. The records are written only in units of 10,000 people, so they are always multiples of 10,000. January is 3,420,000 people, February is 3,520,000 people, and March is 3,620,000 people. Mina said, “It is going up by 100,000 people a month, so April will definitely be 3,720,000 people!”
y-m-10-06.thinking.0: Judging how certain a prediction based on a rule is
y-m-10-06.thinking.2: Writing a prediction and a firm claim as different things
y-m-10-06.prereq.0: Reading and writing large numbers in units of hundred-thousands and millions (4th-grade level)
y-m-10-06.prereq.1: Skip counting by a fixed number
y-m-10-06.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most suitable thought about what Mina said?
y-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find how many people it went up by from January to February and from February to March.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one situation in which April could have a different value (for example, weather or an event), and think about whether the records alone can tell you that.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.a: Around 3,720,000 people is a natural prediction, but a different value could come out
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.a: You read the rule from the records and also told a prediction apart from a certainty.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.b: 3,720,000 people is definitely right. Because it went up by 100,000 in all three months
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.b: From the fact that it was the same three times, you concluded that it will always be so. Think about whether there is evidence that it will be the same the fourth time too.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.c: April cannot be known at all. The first three records are useless for predicting
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.c: You threw away all the earlier records. Think about whether they are a clue to the rule.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.o.d: It seems to be around 3,620,000 people, but it could be wrong
y-m-10-06.s.s1.r.d: You spoke carefully, but you did not use the amount of increase that can be read from the records.
y-m-10-06.s.s1.explain: That it went up by 100,000 over three months is a clue that it is likely to go up by a similar amount in April too. But the amount of increase in April could be different, so you cannot say 'definitely'. Throwing away all the records (c) or ignoring the amount of increase (d) is also not a good prediction.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.prompt: Make records that show Mina's 'definitely' can be wrong. In January, February, and March the number goes up by 100,000 each, and in April it is not 100,000 more than March. All the records are seven-digit numbers, and January and April are multiples of 10,000. Make two records with different changes in April.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.0: Keep the first three months the same as the example, and think of a value for April that is not 100,000 more than March.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing the April value, check that the difference from March is not 100,000 and that it is a multiple of 10,000.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All the records are seven-digit numbers.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The records must be seven-digit numbers from 1,000,000 to 9,999,999.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c2: January and April are multiples of 10,000.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c2: January and April must be written in units of 10,000 people (multiples of 10,000).
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c3: It went up by 100,000 people from January to February.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c3: February must be 100,000 greater than January.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c4: It went up by 100,000 people from February to March.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c4: March must be 100,000 greater than February.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.ok.c5: In April it did not go up by 100,000 people. Mina's 'definitely' is broken.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.fail.c5: April is exactly 100,000 greater than March. Then Mina's words are exactly right.
y-m-10-06.s.s2.explain: For example, 3,420,000 → 3,520,000 → 3,620,000 → 3,730,000 went up by 100,000 for the first three months and then went up by 110,000 in April. A record that goes down, like 5,100,000 → 5,200,000 → 5,300,000 → 5,250,000, is also a counterexample. If even one such record is possible, the records of three months alone cannot make April 'definitely' something.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.prompt: How would you predict the number of people in April? Write your predicted number and the reason, and also write what you would need to know more about to help if your prediction could be wrong.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.0: Put the records you made in s2 next to the original three records, and see how April could have been different from the same records through March.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think of one case in which your prediction would be wrong, and write what information you would need to know it.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I predict that April will be around ... people. Because ...
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain how your predicted number came from the records?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your wording show that your prediction is 'around', not 'definitely'?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is what you would like to know more about something specific that could change your prediction?
y-m-10-06.s.s3.model.0: I predict April will be around 3,720,000 people. That is because it went up by 100,000 each month from January to March. But events or weather in April may have been different, so I would need to know more about that to be sure.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.model.1: I guess about 3,720,000 people, but I cannot say it is definitely so. It is true that the same amount was added for three months, but April may have changed differently. If I also had the May record, I could trust the rule more.
y-m-10-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It does not make the prediction a firm claim, and it says specifically which extra records are needed.
